summary.text: The fall of the Western Roman Empire was the loss of central political control, as the empire failed to enforce its rule and its territory was divided among several successor polities.
Pressure from invading peoples contributed greatly, and climatic changes and diseases drove many of the immediate factors.
Its causes and dating are still debated, and some scholars stress cultural continuity, with 476 as one convenient marker for the end.

items.prompt: In 376 a large group of Goths and others, fleeing the Huns, enters the Empire. What was unusual about Rome's response?

options.label: Rome welcomed them and gave them seats in the Senate
Rome quickly pushed them back across the border
Roman forces could not destroy, expel or subdue them as usual
Rome paid them to fight the Huns for it

items.explain: Roman forces were unable to exterminate, expel or subjugate them, as was their normal practice.

items.prompt: When Theodosius I died in 395, what state did he leave the Empire in?

options.label: A weak army and an Empire divided between warring ministers
A strong army and an Empire united under one heir
A peaceful Empire with the Goths pushed back
An Empire already split by barbarian kingdoms across the West

items.explain: He left a collapsing field army, and the Empire divided between the warring ministers of his two incapable sons.

items.prompt: By the time Odoacer removed the last Western emperor, what was the office worth?

options.label: It still commanded a large army and a full treasury
It carried negligible military, political or financial power
It had passed to the Eastern emperor years before
It was shared among several Germanic kings

items.explain: By 476 the position wielded negligible military, political or financial power and had no effective control over the scattered Western domains.

items.prompt: Writers have said the decline began under Constantine, the soldier emperors, Commodus, even Augustus. What does that spread show?

options.label: Scholars have found no evidence of any decline
All of those rulers lost territory in the same year
The fall began in one agreed year but its cause is disputed
Decline has been stretched over a far wider span than a century

items.explain: The theme of decline has been taken to cover a much wider time span than the hundred years from 376.

items.prompt: A scholar argues the Roman Mediterranean economy carried on after the invasions. What does he suggest was the true break with antiquity?

options.label: The Germanic invasions of the Empire
The deposing of the last Western emperor
The Muslim conquests
The Antonine Plague

items.explain: Pirenne pointed to the continuity of the Mediterranean economy after the barbarian invasions and suggested only the Muslim conquests were a decisive break.

items.prompt: Some scholars stress that Roman culture and settlement carried on long after 476. What name do they give the period?

options.label: The Dark Age
Late antiquity
The Age of Reason
The Migration Period

items.explain: The period described as late antiquity emphasizes cultural continuity through and beyond the political collapse.

source.title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

paragraphs.heading: What the fall means
paragraphs.text: The fall of the Western Roman Empire, often just called the fall of Rome, meant that the western half of the empire lost central political control. The empire could no longer enforce its rule, and its huge territory was split among several successor states. Growing pressure from invading peoples outside Roman culture played a big part. Changes in climate and disease, both constant and in outbreaks, drove many of the immediate causes.

paragraphs.heading: How it unfolded
paragraphs.text: In 376 a large wave of Goths and other non-Romans, fleeing the Huns, entered the empire. The Roman army could not wipe them out, drive them away or bring them under control, which was its usual practice. When Theodosius I died in 395, after two ruinous civil wars, he left a failing field army and an empire split between the feuding ministers of his two weak sons. More groups crossed the Rhine and other borders, the western armies became small and ineffective, and despite short recoveries central rule was never firmly rebuilt.

paragraphs.heading: The year 476
paragraphs.text: By 476 the western emperor had almost no military, political or financial power, and barbarian kingdoms held much of the old western lands. That year Odoacer, a Germanic king, removed Romulus Augustulus, the last western emperor in Italy, and the Senate passed the imperial insignia on to Zeno, the eastern emperor. The western empire never again had the strength to rise. The Eastern Roman, or Byzantine, Empire lived on as a real power in the eastern Mediterranean for centuries, though weaker than before.

paragraphs.heading: When did decline begin
paragraphs.text: Why the West collapsed is a major question for historians of the ancient world, and the answers feed modern talk about why states fail. All agree that the West lost central control and the East lost strength, but the idea of decline has been stretched far beyond the century that began in 376. Cassius Dio saw the accession of Commodus in 180 CE as a fall from an age of gold to one of rust and iron. Others have traced the start to Constantine the Great, to the soldier emperors of 235 to 284, or even to Augustus. The year 476 is a convenient end point, but others have been put forward, such as Rome being sacked in 410 or Julius Nepos dying in 480.

paragraphs.heading: Gibbon's account
paragraphs.text: Gibbon's landmark work soon became the standard text on the subject, and he was the first to try to explain why an empire falls. He was unsure when decline began, placing its start in different parts of his work anywhere from the age of Julius Caesar to the death of Marcus Aurelius. He set the western empire's end in 476, with the removal of the one he called the helpless Augustulus. He opened a long argument over the role of Christianity, but he also gave great weight to other causes of decay inside the empire and to attacks from outside.

paragraphs.heading: A story of continuity
paragraphs.text: The fall is not the only way to frame these events. From at least the time of Henri Pirenne, who lived from 1862 to 1935, scholars have argued that Roman culture and political legitimacy lasted long after 476. Pirenne moved the end of classical civilization to the 8th century, denied that Germanic barbarians had ended the western empire, and stressed that the Roman Mediterranean economy carried on; for him only the Muslim conquests made a decisive break. The newer idea of late antiquity stresses change within a continuing culture, and archaeology now traces continuity in material culture and settlement as late as the eleventh century.
